title: When I need to moderate user-generated content and enforce community guidelines, I want to automatic
target_user: Community Moderator / Admin / Stack Exchange Moderator / Discord Server Administrator
job_to_be_done: When I need to moderate user-generated content and enforce community guidelines, I want to automatically detect and handle spam, abuse, plagiarism, and policy violations, so I can maintain a healthy community without manual review burnout.
painful_workflow: Manually reviewing all user reports, flags, and comments for spam, abuse, off-topic content, or plagiarism. Moderators must work through queues manually, cross-reference user IDs with external databases, and log decisions in separate spreadsheets.
current_workaround: Relying on community flagging and manual review of flagged comments, using browser extensions or custom scripts for bulk actions, and using external search engines for plagiarism checks. For Discord, using built-in audit logs and manual copy-pasting of user IDs into spreadsheets.

competitors.name: SmokeDetector (Charcoal)
competitors.notes: Specifically built for Stack Exchange spam detection, uses AI and crowdsourced feedback. Only covers spam on SE network, no other platforms.
competitors.feature_overlap: Spam detection across multiple SE sites, auto-flagging, user reputation cross-referencing on SE.
competitors.market_positioning: Unofficial Stack Exchange community spam fighting bot

competitors.name: MEE6
competitors.notes: Discord bot with auto-moderation commands, custom filters, and user management. Limited to Discord only.
competitors.feature_overlap: Auto-moderation, custom rule sets, spam filters, user warnings, logging.
competitors.market_positioning: All-in-one Discord bot for moderation, leveling, and engagement

competitors.name: Dyno Bot
competitors.notes: Popular Discord moderation bot with auto-mod, custom commands, and ban management. No cross-platform capabilities.
competitors.feature_overlap: Auto-moderation (spam, mentions, links), custom moderation rules, logging.
competitors.market_positioning: Customizable Discord bot for moderation and administration

competitors.name: Hive Moderation
competitors.notes: AI-driven content moderation API for text, image, and video. Could be integrated to build a dashboard but no out-of-box cross-platform queue.
competitors.feature_overlap: Automated detection of spam, toxicity, NSFW, violence, and policy violations via API.
competitors.market_positioning: Enterprise-grade AI moderation for platforms and apps

competitors.name: CleanSpeak (Inversoft)
competitors.notes: Profanity filtering and moderation platform for user-generated content. Provides a moderation queue but designed for single-platform integration, not multi-community aggregation.
competitors.feature_overlap: Automated text moderation, manual review queue, appeal management, user sanctions.
competitors.market_positioning: Enterprise content moderation and filter for web and mobile apps

competitors.name: Stack Exchange Mod Tools
competitors.notes: Built-in flag queue, moderator dashboard, spam/offensive auto-flagging (via SmokeDetector integration). No connection to Discord.
competitors.feature_overlap: Flag queue, spam detection, user history, moderator actions, reports.
competitors.market_positioning: Native moderation system for Stack Exchange/Stack Overflow

competitors.name: Automoderator (Reddit)
competitors.notes: Configurable rule engine for Reddit subreddits. Illustrates platform-native auto-mod but limited to Reddit.
competitors.feature_overlap: Automated content removal based on keywords, user age/karma, regex; spam filtering.

competitors.name: ModSquad
competitors.notes: Managed human moderation service for many platforms. Not a software tool for community moderators; they act as outsourced moderators.
competitors.feature_overlap: Handles spam, abuse, content review across multiple platforms, but as a service.
competitors.market_positioning: Outsourced moderation and community management services

competitors.name: Perspective API
competitors.notes: Toxicity and profanity scoring API. Could be used to build a moderation frontend but doesn't manage queues or multiple platforms.
competitors.feature_overlap: AI toxicity and abuse detection, scoring for messages.
competitors.market_positioning: Machine learning API for understanding toxicity in online conversations

competitors.name: Copyscape
competitors.notes: Plagiarism checker for web content. Not a moderation dashboard; requires manual checks. Could be integrated via API.
competitors.feature_overlap: Detects duplicate content (plagiarism) across the web.
competitors.pricing: Copyscape Premium starts at $0.05 per search
competitors.market_positioning: Online plagiarism detection for websites and blogs

competitors.name: Carl-bot
competitors.notes: Discord bot with moderation features, reaction roles, and logging. Limited to Discord, no cross-platform support.
competitors.feature_overlap: Auto-mod, spam detection, custom command to check users, logging.
competitors.market_positioning: Multipurpose Discord bot with advanced moderation capabilities

substitutes: Browser extensions like 'Stack Exchange Mod Override' or custom Tampermonkey scripts for bulk actions
Manual spreadsheet tracking + community flags (current workaround)
General AI moderation APIs (Azure Content Moderator, AWS Rekognition for images, not text-only focused)
Plagiarism checkers integrated via manual copy-paste (Grammarly, Turnitin)
Community management platforms like Discourse (includes trust levels, auto-flagging) but requires migration
Open-source scripts on GitHub for Discord ban sync (e.g., cross-server ban list bots) but no unified UI
verified_facts: The four cited signals describe manual moderation workflows on dev.to, Discord forums, and Stack Exchange (flag queues, comment review, plagiarism checks, spreadsheet logging).
SIG-001 with source SRC-001 is listed twice for two different ecosystems, so the claimed '4 independent sources' overstates source independence.
No signal contains quantified data: no time costs, queue volumes, burnout statements, or spending.
Only 2 source types are represented (github, forum).
inferences: Moderation work recurs daily in active communities, making frequency the strongest dimension.
The target users are predominantly unpaid volunteers (Discord admins, SE moderators), which structurally eliminates willingness to pay at the individual level.

Free, entrenched incumbents already cover most of this JTBD: Discord AutoMod and free bots (MEE6, Dyno, Carl-bot), Reddit AutoModerator, Stack Exchange's community-run SmokeDetector/Charcoal for spam, and Forem's built-in moderation for dev.to — inferred from market knowledge, not from the provided evidence.
The 'manual' nature of the work partly reflects moderation's inherent need for human judgment on edge cases, not purely a tooling gap.
assumptions: That communities would adopt and trust a third-party cross-platform moderation tool over native/free options.
That the described manual workflows are not already handled by existing bots or platform features unknown to the signal authors.
That SRC-001 cited for Discord and SRC-001 cited for Stack Exchange are distinct documents rather than a duplicate.
unknowns: Queue volumes, time spent per moderator per day, and moderator attrition/burnout rates.
Whether any of these communities or their owners have ever paid for moderation tooling.
Actual size and activity level of the communities behind each signal.
Whether the double-cited SRC-001 represents one or two sources.
Who the economic buyer would be (server owner? community? platform?) — no evidence addresses this.
